---
title: "The Audit Pipeline: Making Your Adjustments Defensible"
---

When you run your data through SPARMVET, there are tiers: **T1** (the data joined per your data
analysis recipe, after the tier-1 steps), **T2** (the standard transformations every plot in your
recipe shares) and **T3** (the table one plot is drawn from: T2 plus that plot's own steps of the
recipe). The Home header gives you **two choices**:

- **Mode** (only when your setup switches the audit on): **Exploration** (look at the data; one
  plot, the Result; nothing is saved) or **Audit** (create audit steps; the plot becomes the
  audited plot).
- **Table to view**: **Source** (a source table as read from its file), **T1**, **T2** or **T3**.
  In Audit mode, T1, T2 and T3 are the audited tables where an audit step changes them.

**Audit mode** is where you remove bad samples, drop unused columns, and filter to the rows you
want to publish. The audit pipeline is what records every decision you commit in Audit mode so
your final figures are reproducible and defensible. Every change you commit is captured as an
**audit node** — a small record that says *what* you changed, *which plots* it applies to, and
(mandatory) *why* you made the change. Together, the audit nodes form your audit trail.

## Original recipe and audit recipe (confirmed by Eve, 2026-11-15)

1. HOME opens the original recipe. It is the reference. HOME never changes it.
2. Only Blueprint can edit a recipe.
3. When you audit, HOME works on a copy of the original recipe. This copy is the audit recipe.
4. The steps of the original recipe are in the copy. You cannot edit them or remove them.
5. In the audit you can only add steps: remove rows, or remove a column. Each step has a reason.
6. A step you added can be removed again. It leaves the audit recipe. The original recipe is not touched.
7. The export is the audit recipe: the original steps plus the audit steps that are still in it.
8. The original plot stays beside the audited plot, so you can see what the audit changed.

## Why this matters for publication

When you submit a paper, a reviewer or editor may ask: "Why did you remove sample S2?" Without the audit pipeline, your answer is "I remember… I think it was the contamination." With the audit pipeline, the answer is in the exported report:

> ⚠️ **[Primary key affected]** Excluded sample `S2` from all plots (reason: poor sequencing quality, see lab notebook entry 2026-04-12).

Every removal is named, dated, and justified. You take responsibility for the decision; the report makes that responsibility visible.

## How to author audit decisions

In **Audit** mode, with **T3** viewed, the left sidebar is your only authoring surface (on another table the panel says "To create an audit step, view T3."):

- The **filter builder** (button labelled "➜ Send to Audit (N)") — turn the rows you've staged into audit nodes.
- The **column selector above the data preview** ("➜ Audit drops (N)" button) — turn deselected columns into `drop_column` audit nodes.

The right sidebar is the **audit panel**: it shows the audit decisions for the *currently active plot*. Every decision lives there with its reason text-box. Until you fill in a reason, the bottom **Apply** button stays locked. Once you Apply, the decisions move from "pending" to "committed" and the change is reflected in the data.

To remove an audit decision, click the 🗑 next to it. The data immediately reappears (audit nodes only ever *remove* data; deleting a node is the only "undo").

## Per-plot vs. all-plots: the propagation choice

Most adjustments only make sense on one plot. If you filter "value > 90" on a similarity plot, that doesn't apply to your QC plot — they have different data. So by default, every audit decision is **per-plot only**. Switching plots in T3 mode shows you a different audit panel.

**But sometimes a decision should propagate.** A clear example: if sample `S2` has poor sequencing quality, you'll want to remove it from every plot — except possibly the QC contamination plot, which is precisely where you'd point a reviewer to *show* that S2 was bad.

When you author an audit decision that's eligible for propagation, SPARMVET shows you a small dialog with three choices:

- **This plot only** — the default, fastest path. Applies just to the plot you're currently looking at.
- **All plots** — the decision is copied into every plot's audit panel. New plots added to your data analysis recipe later will *not* automatically inherit this decision; you'd need to re-propagate.
- **All plots except…** — pick which plots to skip. This is the "remove S2 everywhere except the QC contamination plot" case.

Linked deletion: if you've propagated to multiple plots and later click 🗑 on the node in *any* of those plots, the node is removed from *all* of them. The audit pipeline thinks of a propagated node as one decision applied many places, not many independent decisions.

## Where the step is written: at this plot, or at a table it is built from

The three choices above write the step at the **tier 3 of each plot** (the last step of the plot's own table). A fourth choice acts **earlier in the recipe**:

- **At a table this plot is built from** — the step is written at the tier 1 (or the tier 2) of a table the plot is built from, for example the table *ResFinder*. Every table and every plot built from that table is then built again from it, and they all show the audited result. The dialog lists each table with what is built from it ("2 other tables and 5 plots are built from it"), so you see how far the step reaches before you confirm. "Built from it" does not say that the table changes: the plot badge tells you afterwards, for each plot, whether its table changed or is the same as the original.

#### Choosing the place on the "Path of the data"

In Audit mode, below the strip at the top of HOME, the panel **Path of the data** (closed until you open it) shows the tables and the plots of the recipe as a list and as a map of dots, with arrows from a table to what is built from it. Hover or focus a table to read what it is and what is built from it; click it (or press Enter) to choose it as the place of your step. Choose one place for each independent graph, or press **All original tables of this group**. What is built from the chosen place is marked. Then press **Create an audit step here...**: the dialog of *Send to Audit* opens with your place ticked (build the filter in the Filters panel first, with the table of a plot in view T3). The switch **Around my selection** hides everything that is neither upstream nor downstream of your choice. A table that no plot reads is a place too: choose it and the panel offers a small form for a filter on that table; the table changes and no figure does, and the audited table is in the export made in Audit mode.

  The places are listed as the path of the lineage, from the original tables down to your plot, each line indented by how far down the path it is; the plot's own tier 3 is the last line. You choose one place on a path. As soon as you tick a place, the places below it are shown greyed with a "~" ("follows from the place chosen above"): they are built from the one you chose and cannot be chosen too; the places above it cannot be chosen either. Untick it and they are free again. Several original tables that feed the plot each start their own path, so you may tick the first place of each. (The words on screen are provisional.)
- You choose **one place on a path**. A table and a table built from it cannot both be chosen in one step, and neither can a table and the plot built from it (the list also holds the line "Plot … (tier 3)"); the dialog says which two. The first tables of several *original* tables may be chosen together. Two separate decisions at different places are fine: they are applied tier by tier (tier 1, then tier 2, then tier 3), and inside a tier in the order you wrote them.
- Only the tables that hold the column of your step are listed.
- A drop of a column that a later join reads as a key is refused at its place, with the join named.

A typical case: the app adds a line "missing in original table" for a sample that has no ResFinder result (its marker column `ResFinder_not_in_original_data` is true). To leave these lines out of every analysis built from ResFinder, filter on the marker at the **tier 1 of ResFinder**, with your reason. The plots that read those lines lose them; a plot that does not read them keeps its table and says so in its badge; a plot built from other tables is not touched.

The audit card says where the step is written. **Compare** shows the original plot beside the audited one. In Audit mode the **T1**, **T2** and **T3** views show the **audited** tables where an audit step changes them: the badge says "Viewing: T1, audited". A table that no step changes shows the original, and the badge says "Viewing: T1, original" with "no audit step changes this table". **Source** is always the file as read, and in Exploration mode every view shows the original. The 🗑 of the card removes the step and every table and plot is built again without it. In the export, the data file of each plot built from the table is the audited table, `t3_steps.yaml` lists the step with its place (`steps_by_place`), the README and the report say where it is written and why, and the reproducibility recipe holds it as a plain step at the end of that tier (for a step at a plot: in the plot's own tier-3 steps).

### The table files of an export made in Audit mode

When you export while you are in **Audit** mode, every table that an audit step changes (the table of the place and every table built from it) comes **twice** in the bundle: the original, `T1_data.tsv`, and the audited one beside it, `T1_data_audited.tsv` (and `T2_data_audited.tsv` for a tier 2). The original is unchanged. A table that no step changes has only its original, and a step written at a plot changes no table, only that plot's `T3_data_<plot>.tsv`. The README and the report tell, for each table, which file is which and which steps made the difference. When you export in **Exploration** mode the table files are the originals only, whatever audit steps exist (the plots and the plot's T3 file are always audited); the README says so.

### The audit recipe of an export made in Audit mode

An export made in **Audit** mode also holds the **audit recipe**, in the folder `audit_recipe/`, as `<recipe id>_audited.yaml`. It is the original recipe with every audit step written at its place (the end of the tier you wrote it at), each step with its reason, its audit id and its day in its own comment, so no step is hidden. It is a recipe like any other: put the file in the recipes folder with the data it reads (its data references are the original's, the data files are not copied) and the app opens it and runs it on its own, with no session. Running it gives the audited tables at every tier and the audited Result data (T3) of every plot of that export. The README and the report say where it is.

### Propagation preview — read it before you confirm

Before you click *Add to audit pipeline*, the modal shows a per-plot preview of where the filter will actually land:

> 📍 **Propagation preview:** ✅ 5 apply  •  ⚠️ 2 skip (col missing)
>
> ▶ Show details
>   ⚠️ *Plasmid Prevalence by Country* — column not in the Result data (T3) of this plot; will be SKIPPED
>   ⚠️ *Phenotype Genome Length* — column not in the Result data (T3) of this plot; will be SKIPPED
>
> 👉 Apply filters one at a time and verify each plot before stacking. A skipped plot is **NOT filtered** — it shows the unfiltered data.

**Three states per target plot:**

- ✅ **column present** → the filter will apply
- ⚠️ **column absent** → the filter is silently skipped on that plot (the plot shows unfiltered data; verify it's what you want)
- ❓ **dataset unknown** → SPARMVET couldn't find the table that plot reads; verify by hand after applying

**Why "apply one at a time"?** When you author multiple filters and propagate them in batch, every skipped plot becomes a question: *did the user mean to skip it, or did they not realise their filter wouldn't take effect there?* By applying one filter, switching tabs, and verifying the effect before authoring the next, you build an honest, defensible audit trail.

### One-at-a-time review workflow

This is the recommended sequence for building a clean audit trail:

1. **Stage one filter** in the Filters accordion. Don't stage others yet.
2. **Click "➜ Send to Audit (1)"**. The propagation modal opens.
3. **Read the preview**. Check which plots show ✅, which show ⚠️ (column absent). If a plot you expected to be affected shows ⚠️, that means the column name differs in the table that plot reads — fix the source data or author the filter separately for that plot with the correct column name.
4. **Choose scope** — "This plot only", "All plots", or "All plots except…". When in doubt, start with "This plot only" and expand scope once you've confirmed the effect.
5. **Fill in the reason** in the right sidebar audit panel (see [Writing good reasons](#writing-good-reasons) below). The Apply button stays locked until a reason is entered.
6. **Click Apply**. The node commits. Verify the data preview and the plot on the current plot sub-tab.
7. **Switch to every other affected plot** (check the tabs that showed ✅ in the preview). Confirm the filter took effect as expected.
8. **Only then** return to the Filters accordion and stage the next filter.

Stacking multiple uncommitted nodes before verifying any of them is the most common way to end up with an audit trail that's technically complete but analytically opaque.

### Writing good reasons {#writing-good-reasons}

The reason field is the only free-text part of the audit trail. It's what a reviewer reads when they ask "why was this sample removed?" The quality of the reason determines whether your audit is reproducible or just formally complete.

**Good reasons** are specific and reference external evidence:

- `Poor sequencing quality (Q30 < 40%). See lab notebook 2026-04-12.`
- `Duplicate — same isolate as ST22_032, sequenced twice in run 7.`
- `Outlier identified in QC review meeting 2026-05-02. Excluded from analytical plots, retained in QC plots.`
- `Similarity threshold for publication: ≥ 90% identity, per Methods section 2.3.`

**Weak reasons** are vague and non-reproducible:

- `Bad sample.` — what made it bad? by whose judgement? when?
- `Not relevant.` — to what? on what grounds?
- `Test.` — don't commit test nodes; use "Reset filters" instead.

The reason isn't just for others — it's for you in six months when you're responding to reviewer comments. A reason that would satisfy a reviewer is the right bar to aim for.

## Primary keys — extra care needed

A **primary key** is a column that links your tables together. In a typical SPARMVET project the primary key is `sample_id`; in long-format AMR data, gene identifiers can also serve as join keys. SPARMVET detects primary keys automatically from your data analysis recipe's join steps.

When you target a primary key with an audit decision, SPARMVET applies extra rules:

### Dropping a primary-key column is **blocked where a later join still uses it**

You can't add a `drop_column` node for a join key (for example `sample_id`) when a later join of your recipe still uses that column: the link between your tables would break. The refusal is given for that place only. Where no later join uses the column, for example a drop in a plot's own steps, the drop is allowed. Steps written in the recipe itself are never refused. If you click "➜ Audit drops" with such a primary key in the deselected list, the message names the join that needs the column and says to use a row filter or row exclusion instead.

If your need is to *anonymize* the IDs in the published report (e.g. the journal asks you not to expose internal sample IDs), that is a different problem and currently outside SPARMVET's scope. For now, the report shows whatever IDs your data analysis recipe uses; consider relabelling samples *before* assembly if anonymization is a hard requirement.

### Filtering rows on a primary key is **allowed** (with a warning)

You *can* filter on a primary-key column — for example `sample_id == "S2"` to keep only that sample. SPARMVET keeps the node as a regular `filter_row` and **does not silently convert it** to an exclusion. The semantics are: the operator does exactly what it says (`eq` keeps the matched value; `ne`/`not_in` excludes it).

A ⚠️ **Primary key** banner is added to the node automatically, both in the modal and in the right-sidebar audit panel, to remind you that this decision changes which samples flow into joined plots downstream.

If your intent is *exclusion* ("remove S2 from everything"), use `ne` or `not_in` directly — the audit will then read as "rows removed where `sample_id == S2`" which is exactly the right framing for a methods section.

> Earlier behaviour (pre-2026-04-30) silently converted `eq`/`in` on a PK to `ne`/`not_in` — that turned "select X" into "remove X" without a clear UI cue and was confusing. The current rule is: **the operator is the truth**; the warning is the safety rail.

### The primary-key warning is permanent

Every audit node that targeted a primary key carries a `⚠️ Primary key — Primary ID/Key alignment` banner in the audit panel. The same warning persists into the exported report:

> ⚠️ **[Primary key affected]** Excluded sample `S2` from all plots…

This is **not** an error or a complaint — it's a marker for you and your readers: "this decision changes which samples appear across joined plots; the user owns this decision". It's expected to be present in many real audit reports.

## When *not* to use a primary-key exclusion

Sometimes the user's instinct is "remove sample S2 from this plot" when the actual analytical intent is different. Common case:

> "I'm looking at a long-format gene-similarity table. I only want similarities ≥ 90%. Sample S2 doesn't have any genes meeting that bar so I'll just exclude S2."

Don't do that. The correct framing is: *filter on the `value` column where `value >= 90`*. The effect on the visualization may be the same (S2 disappears) but the audit trail is meaningfully different:

- **Wrong**: "Excluded sample S2." → reader thinks S2 was a bad sample.
- **Right**: "Filtered to similarity ≥ 90." → reader understands S2 simply had no similarities meeting the threshold.

The first hides analytical context the reader needs. The second is honest. SPARMVET's automatic conversion of primary-key filters to exclusions only triggers when you explicitly target the key column — so as long as you build your filter on the `value` column instead, no conversion happens.

## Use cases summary

To make the rules concrete, these are the cases the design accommodates:

**Case A — Bad sample, but keep it on the plot that justifies the removal.**
Sample `S2` had poor quality. You want it gone from your analytical figures, *but* you want the QC contamination plot to still show S2's high contamination bar so your report can point to that plot as evidence.
→ Author the exclusion → propagate to **All plots except…** → select the QC plot in the multiselect.

**Case B — Wrong sample, remove everywhere.**
You discover S2 was mis-labelled or contaminated upstream. It shouldn't be in any plot.
→ Author the exclusion → propagate to **All plots**.

**Case C — Long-format value filter (not a sample-ID exclusion).**
Your long-format table has rows like `(sample, gene, similarity)`. You want similarity ≥ 90.
→ Build the filter on the `similarity` column, not on `sample`. Per-plot scope is fine. No primary-key warning fires (similarity isn't a join key). If S2 ends up with no rows, the audit correctly says "filtered to similarity ≥ 90" rather than "excluded S2".

## Saving and restoring your work

Every time you click **Apply**, your committed audit decisions are saved to a **T3 ghost** file alongside the assembly results. If you close SPARMVET and come back later with the same data analysis recipe and the same data files, the ghost is restored automatically — your audit decisions reappear in their per-plot panels exactly as you left them.

If your data files have changed since the last session, SPARMVET notices and warns you: the assembly is rebuilt, but the audit decisions persist (a row filter on `sample_id == S2` keeps applying as long as `sample_id` exists in the new data; the audit pipeline doesn't care that the assembly was redone).

If you restructure your data analysis recipe — rename a plot, remove a plot — any audit nodes that target the missing plot become **orphaned**. SPARMVET tells you about them at restore time and lists them in an "Orphaned" section so you can re-target or delete them. They never apply silently; you always make a deliberate choice.

## The bottom line

The audit pipeline is built around one principle: **every analytical decision should be defensible, traceable, and named**. T3 mode is where you turn raw data into the figures that tell your scientific story; the audit pipeline is the receipts file that proves you didn't fabricate or over-massage that story.

The cost is: filling in a reason every time you remove a sample or drop a column. The payoff is: when a reviewer asks "why did you exclude S2", you can hand them the exported report and the answer is right there, in your own words, with the timestamp.

## Appendix: Filter operators reference

The filter builder in the left sidebar adapts its widgets to the column type:

### Numeric columns (`Int*`, `Float*`, `Decimal`)

| Op       | Symbol | Widget                | Polars semantics                       |
|----------|--------|-----------------------|----------------------------------------|
| `eq`     | `=`    | numeric input         | `col == value`                         |
| `ne`     | `≠`    | numeric input         | `col != value`                         |
| `gt`     | `>`    | numeric input         | `col > value`                          |
| `ge`     | `≥`    | numeric input         | `col >= value`                         |
| `lt`     | `<`    | numeric input         | `col < value`                          |
| `le`     | `≤`    | numeric input         | `col <= value`                         |
| `between`| `↔`    | two numeric inputs (min, max) + inclusivity radio | `col.is_between(lo, hi, closed=...)` |

The **`between`** operator says which ends of the range are included, with four choices:

- both ends included (default) → `closed='both'` → audit shows `col ∈ [lo, hi]`
- min included, max not → `closed='left'` → `col ∈ [lo, hi)`
- max included, min not → `closed='right'` → `col ∈ (lo, hi]`
- neither end included → `closed='none'` → `col ∈ (lo, hi)`

The choice is carried to the audit step, the export and the report ("between 90 and 99, the lower end included, the upper end not"). If the user enters `lo > hi`, SPARMVET auto-swaps them rather than producing an empty filter.

**The value has the type of its column.** The panel shows what the column holds ("year holds whole numbers (Int64)") and keeps the real value: a number for a number column, true or false for a true/false column, text for text. The list of values comes from the whole column, not from its first rows. A number column that the plot uses as a discrete axis offers the list operators (`∈`, `∉`, `=`, `≠`, a list is picked) and also the comparisons (`>`, `≥`, `<`, `≤`, `↔`), which use number boxes, so that "> 1998 and < 2003" can be written. A step saved before the real value was kept holds the value as text; it is read from the type the step carries when it is shown and exported, and a value that cannot be read is reported, never guessed.

### Categorical / discrete columns

| Op        | Symbol | Widget                  | Polars semantics                |
|-----------|--------|-------------------------|---------------------------------|
| `in`      | `∈`    | selectize multi-pick    | `col.is_in([v1, v2, ...])`      |
| `not_in`  | `∉`    | selectize multi-pick    | `~col.is_in([v1, v2, ...])`     |
| `eq`      | `=`    | selectize multi-pick    | (auto-promoted to `in` when multiple values selected) |
| `ne`      | `≠`    | selectize multi-pick    | (auto-promoted to `not_in` when multiple values selected) |

Set-membership comparisons cast both sides to string, so a numeric column declared `discrete` (via `scale_x_discrete` in the data analysis recipe) still works with the selectize picker.

### Auto-promotion rules

The filter row stores a single `op` field but the underlying logic adapts when the value is a list:

- `op="eq"` with a list → upgraded to `op="in"`
- `op="ne"` with a list → upgraded to `op="not_in"`

This is intentional — picking multiple values from the selectize implies set membership.

### Type coercion (defensive)

Numeric column + string operand (e.g. user typed `"2022"` for a Float64 year column) — the apply-time coercion converts the string to the column's native dtype. Both filter paths (data preview and plot render) do this identically.

If a string operand reaches a numeric column despite the dtype-aware widgets, a warning fires in the server log:

```
[filter] ⚠️ string operand on numeric column 'year' (Float64); coercing '2022'
```

This means the widget bypassed its own type contract; not user-facing but worth flagging in dev.

### Regression test

The end-to-end operator contract is locked down by `app/tests/test_filter_operators.py` (21 cases covering every op × value-shape × dtype combination). Run from the repo root:

```bash
pytest app/tests/test_filter_operators.py -v
```
